title: A useful pilot that couldn’t be evaluated: the museum route lacked outcome measurement
description: The museum created and distributed a printed indoor route for visitors when the sculpture garden flooded, but the pilot recorded distribution (38 copies) and a small operational change (a start sign) while explicitly not tracking whether visitors completed the route or were satisfied. The central point: the experiment produced implementation facts but no outcome data, limiting lessons that can be drawn from the pilot.
audience: Museum operations managers, visitor services teams, front‑of‑house supervisors
rationale: Many museums run small, low‑cost pilots to handle weather or capacity interruptions. This example shows how a simple intervention can be implemented quickly yet leave a critical evaluation gap — useful evidence for teams planning short pilots to include basic measurement (completion, satisfaction) so they can judge effectiveness and iterate responsibly.
evidence: Explicit facts in the source: “the front desk can give visitors a free printed route…”; “In April, the museum handed out the route at two wet Sunday openings. The desk counted 38 copies handed out.” Crucially: “Staff recorded no systematic counts of how many visitors completed the route and did not track visitor satisfaction.” Also: “At the first opening some visitors asked where to start, so a sign was added by the desk at the second.”

title: Designing the indoor alternative for accessibility: step‑free routing matters
description: The printed indoor route intentionally follows step‑free public corridors from front desk to café, showing that accessibility was considered when providing an indoor alternative for visitors whose garden visit was disrupted. The central insight: an alternate route can be designed to preserve accessibility priorities rather than simply redirecting visitors without regard to mobility needs.
audience: Accessibility coordinators, exhibition planners, curators responsible for visitor experience
rationale: When outdoor spaces close, how a museum routes visitors indoors affects who can continue to use the space. Highlighting that the route follows step‑free corridors provides a concrete example for other institutions planning contingencies to maintain accessible options.
evidence: Source states the route “starts at the front desk and ends at the café. It follows step‑free public corridors.” The note is explicitly “for visitors whose plans included the sculpture garden” and intended “to help visitors adapt their visit when the garden is closed.”

title: Small, rapid iteration in front‑of‑house practice: add a start sign after observing confusion
description: During the two wet‑opening pilots, staff observed that some visitors didn’t know where to begin the printed route; in response a sign was added by the desk at the second opening. The central insight: simple, observation‑driven fixes (signage at distribution point) can be implemented between pilot sessions to reduce visitor friction.
audience: Front‑of‑house staff, visitor experience designers, small museum teams running pilots
rationale: The detail illustrates a low‑risk operational improvement that can be applied immediately during a pilot. It’s a concrete example of responsive in‑field iteration that other teams can replicate when testing short‑term visitor adjustments.
evidence: Source: “At the first opening some visitors asked where to start, so a sign was added by the desk at the second.” Also confirms distribution channel: “the front desk can give visitors a free printed route… In April, the museum handed out the route at two wet Sunday openings. The desk counted 38 copies handed out.”

title: Practical contingency: using the front desk to distribute printed alternate routes
description: The museum used the front desk as the distribution point for a printed indoor route when the sculpture garden was closed for high water, with the route starting at the desk and ending at the café. The central point: the front desk can serve as an effective, low‑complexity channel to deliver on‑site contingency information to visitors.
audience: Visitor services planners, operations staff at small to mid‑size cultural institutions
rationale: For institutions seeking straightforward ways to communicate last‑minute changes, this shows a minimal logistics model: a printed handout at a staffed point that pairs with a simple sign and same‑day notices. It’s a low‑tech alternative when digital or staffed guidance may not be available.
evidence: Source facts: “When the garden closes for high water, the front desk can give visitors a free printed route… The route starts at the front desk and ends at the café.” Distribution data: “the desk counted 38 copies handed out.”
